issues.legal_issue: An acquisition under the earlier land-acquisition regime lapses under the transitional provision only when, in a qualifying pending proceeding, neither possession has been taken nor compensation has been paid.
material_facts: The cases concerned acquisition proceedings initiated under the earlier land-acquisition regime in which an award had been made at least five years before the replacement regime commenced.
The statutory wording joined two negative conditions: possession had not been taken and compensation had not been paid.
Taking possession under the earlier regime could vest the land in the acquiring authority even if compensation remained unpaid.
issues.conclusion: The two conditions are cumulative: lapse occurs only if possession has not been taken and compensation has not been paid. If either possession has been taken or compensation has been paid, the acquisition does not lapse under this provision.
issues.legal_principle: Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act is an exception to Section 24(1)(b), and applies to qualifying pending proceedings. Where two negative conditions are joined by “or,” the word may be read conjunctively in context; the Court relied on Patel Chunibhai Dajibha v. Narayanrao Khanderao Jambekar, Punjab Produce & Trading Co. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Brown & Co. v. Harrison, and M/s. Ranchhoddas Atmaram v. Union of India. Sections 16, 31 and 34 of the 1894 Act support the distinction between vesting, payment, and the interest consequence of non-payment.

rule.if: transitional_acquisition_proceeding and qualifying_old_award and possession_not_taken and compensation_not_paid

predicates.transitional_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an acquisition begun under an earlier land-acquisition regime and is still pending when a replacement regime takes effect.
predicates.qualifying_old_award: An award was made sufficiently long before the replacement regime took effect to meet the statutory threshold for possible lapse.
predicates.possession_not_taken: The acquiring authority had not taken possession of the acquired land.
predicates.compensation_not_paid: Compensation had not been paid, including by a legally sufficient tender.

issues.definition: When a qualifying pending acquisition has an old award and neither possession nor compensation has been delivered, the acquisition lapses.

issues.legal_issue: A valid tender of compensation satisfies the payment condition even when the landholder refuses to accept the amount.
material_facts: The Court considered acquisitions in which compensation was tendered to the persons entitled to receive it but was refused.
The earlier acquisition regime required the acquiring authority to tender payment and to pay the amount unless prevented by specified circumstances.
issues.conclusion: Compensation is treated as paid when it has been tendered and made available to the person entitled to it; a landholder cannot establish non-payment merely by refusing the tender.
issues.legal_principle: Section 31(1) of the 1894 Act requires tender and payment, while Section 31(2) addresses circumstances preventing payment. The Court construed “paid” in Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act in the context of those provisions and relied on Benares State Bank Ltd. v. CIT, Collector of Central Excise v. Elphinstone Spg. & Wvg. Mills Co. Ltd., and J. Dalmia v. Commissioner of Income Tax.

predicates.transitional_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an acquisition begun under an earlier land-acquisition regime and is still pending when a replacement regime takes effect.
predicates.compensation_tendered_and_available: The acquiring authority offered the compensation unconditionally and made it available to the person entitled to receive it.
predicates.landholder_refused_tender: The person entitled to compensation declined to accept the amount offered.

issues.definition: A refusal does not turn an unconditional, available tender of compensation into non-payment.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to deposit compensation in court does not by itself cause an acquisition to lapse where possession has been taken, although statutory interest may be payable.
material_facts: The earlier regime required a court deposit in specified circumstances, including refusal to accept compensation or a dispute about entitlement or apportionment.
The acquiring authority could take possession and the land could vest in the State despite compensation remaining unpaid or undeposited.
The earlier and replacement regimes provided for interest when compensation was not paid or deposited by the relevant time.
issues.conclusion: Non-deposit in court does not itself lapse the acquisition. Where possession has been taken and compensation remains unpaid or undeposited, the compensation obligation is addressed through interest rather than lapse.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 31(2) and 34 of the 1894 Act provide for court deposit in specified circumstances and interest for failure to pay or deposit; Sections 77 and 80 of the 2013 Act carry forward corresponding provisions. The Court relied on Satendra Prasad Jain v. State of U.P., Tika Ram v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Pratap v. State of Rajasthan in explaining that non-payment does not undo vesting after possession has been taken.

rule.if: transitional_acquisition_proceeding and award_made and possession_taken and compensation_unpaid_and_undeposited

predicates.transitional_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an acquisition begun under an earlier land-acquisition regime and is still pending when a replacement regime takes effect.
predicates.award_made: The acquiring authority made an award determining compensation for the acquired land.
predicates.possession_taken: The acquiring authority took possession of the acquired land.
predicates.compensation_unpaid_and_undeposited: Compensation remained unpaid and was not deposited with the court in circumstances requiring such a deposit.

issues.definition: When possession has been taken after an award, missing payment or court deposit results in an interest obligation rather than lapse of the acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: The proviso concerning compensation for the majority of landholdings forms part of the lapse provision and entitles all relevant beneficiaries to enhanced compensation when its conditions are met.
material_facts: The proviso follows the provision governing lapse and addresses an award for which compensation in respect of a majority of landholdings has not been deposited in the beneficiaries’ accounts.

The Court concluded that possession having been taken prevents lapse even if compensation has not been paid, while non-deposit for the majority of holdings triggers enhanced compensation for all beneficiaries specified in the acquisition notification.
issues.conclusion: The proviso is part of Section 24(2), not Section 24(1)(b). Where compensation for a majority of the landholdings has not been deposited, all beneficiaries specified in the acquisition notification are entitled to compensation under the 2013 Act, without lapse where the requirements for lapse are not both met.
issues.legal_principle: The Court read the proviso with Section 24(2), considering its placement, the colon following that subsection, and the relationship between non-payment, deposit, lapse, and enhanced compensation. It applied principles on the construction of provisos stated in State of Rajasthan v. Leela Jain, Sales-tax Officer v. Hanuman Prasad, and S. Sundaram Pillai v. V.R. Pattabiraman.

predicates.transitional_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an acquisition begun under an earlier land-acquisition regime and is still pending when a replacement regime takes effect.
predicates.qualifying_old_award: An award was made sufficiently long before the replacement regime took effect to meet the statutory threshold for the lapse provision.
predicates.compensation_not_deposited_for_majority_: Compensation for more than half of the landholdings covered by the award was not deposited in the beneficiaries’ accounts.

issues.definition: For a qualifying pending acquisition, failure to deposit compensation for most holdings gives every notified beneficiary the enhanced compensation entitlement.

issues.legal_issue: Taking possession and vesting under the earlier acquisition regime are not undone merely because compensation was not paid or the transitional provision is invoked.
material_facts: The earlier regime provided that, after an award and taking possession, the land vested absolutely in the Government free from encumbrances.
The transitional provision did not expressly provide for divesting land already vested in the Government or transferred to beneficiaries or third parties.
The statutory scheme addressed unpaid compensation through payment and interest provisions.
issues.conclusion: Section 24 does not divest title that has already vested following the taking of possession; non-payment of compensation does not require the acquiring authority to restore possession.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16 of the 1894 Act provides for vesting upon taking possession after an award, while Sections 31 and 34 provide remedies for unpaid compensation. The Court relied on Satendra Prasad Jain v. State of U.P., Gulam Mustafa v. State of Maharashtra, C. Padma v. Deputy Secretary, Northern Indian Glass Industries v. Jaswant Singh, and The Fruit & Vegetable Merchants Union v. The Delhi Improvement Trust in applying the principle that vested title is not undone without provision for divesting.

predicates.earlier_regime_acquisition: The land was acquired through proceedings begun under an earlier land-acquisition regime.
predicates.award_made: The acquiring authority made an award for the acquired land.
predicates.possession_taken_and_title_vested: The acquiring authority took possession in circumstances that vested title to the land in it.

issues.definition: Once possession has been taken and title has vested, invoking the transitional lapse provision does not undo that title.
